message:
Hi David,

I want to address the $50 invoice for "extra communication handling." I don't believe this charge is fair, and I'd like you to waive it.

My communication with you was only necessary because the repair took a month to complete. I reported the leak on June 1, and the part wasn't ordered until June 22 — and only after I followed up multiple times and discovered the plumber hadn't ordered it as promised. I wasn't creating extra work; I was trying to get a leaking sink fixed in a reasonable timeframe.

I'll acknowledge that filing the complaint with the property management company on June 25 without telling you first wasn't my best move — I should have given you a heads-up, and I apologize for not doing so. By that point, though, I was genuinely frustrated after weeks of waiting.

The fee being resolved and this behind us would mean a lot. I've valued being a reliable tenant, and I'd like to keep our working relationship on good footing.

Thanks for considering this.

[Your name]

---

Subject: Sink repair – resolved

Hi Maya,

I want to confirm that the sink repair was completed on July 1. I apologize for the delays — the part availability issue with the plumber was outside what I expected, and I understand the wait was frustrating.

I also want to address the invoice I sent for $50. I've withdrawn it — it wasn't appropriate, and I don't believe any charge is owed for communication related to the repair.

Thanks for your patience while this was being sorted out. If anything else comes up with the unit, please don't hesitate to contact me directly.

Best regards,
[Your name]

Subject: Jake's Stay — Proposed Resolution

Tom,

Thanks for your messages. I acknowledge I was in the wrong by not requesting prior written approval for Jake's stay, and I should have notified you as soon as he moved in on June 1 rather than on June 10. That's on me, and I take the lease terms seriously.

That said, I'd like to ask for a reasonable resolution rather than an escalation. Jake has caused no damage, no noise complaints, and no issues during his stay, and he's close to securing a job and his own housing. I'm proposing the following:

- Jake will move out no later than June 25 (not June 30), giving him time to finalize his housing arrangements.
- I will pay for any additional utility costs attributable to his stay.
- I will inspect the unit with you after he departs to confirm there's no excess wear.
- In the future, I will submit all guest requests in writing in advance, as the lease requires.

If a slightly earlier date works better for you, I'm open to June 22. I'd also note the faucet repair was completed only after a follow-up, which I've documented, though I raise that only for context—not to excuse my own lapse.

I'd like to resolve this amicably and avoid formal proceedings. Please let me know by [date] whether June 22 or 25 works for you.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Unit/address]

---

Subject: Bathroom Mould – Urgent Remediation Required & Reimbursement

Hi Tom,

I'm writing to formally summarize where things stand with the bathroom mould, because the situation has now worsened and needs immediate action.

Timeline for your reference:

- **Mar 1:** I emailed reporting black mould on the bathroom ceiling.
- **Mar 5:** You said a contractor would attend within two weeks.
- **Mar 12:** No contact; I followed up.
- **Mar 20:** Pete inspected, took photos, and said he'd provide a quote by March 27.
- **Mar 27–28:** No quote arrived. Having waited nearly four weeks, I purchased a mould removal kit and cleaned the ceiling myself at my own expense.
- **Apr 2:** You told me the quote was "too high" and you'd look for cheaper options.
- **Apr 10:** The mould has now spread to the wall. I have uploaded dated photos to the property portal.

As the landlord, you have a legal obligation to maintain the property in a habitable condition and address health hazards like mould within a reasonable time. Nearly six weeks have passed since my first report, and the problem is now actively spreading — this is no longer something that can be deferred while comparison-shopping quotes.

What I need from you:

1. **Confirm in writing, within 48 hours, a date for professional remediation** of the mould on the ceiling and wall. "Looking into it" is no longer acceptable given the health risk.
2. **Reimburse me $200** for the mould removal kit and the work I performed, which became necessary only because the repair was not carried out.

Regarding the rent: I proposed deducting $200 to cover these costs. I understand you dispute this, so rather than us continuing to disagree over text, I'm happy to resolve the reimbursement through the proper channels — including a repair-and-deduct claim, a complaint to the local housing authority/rent board, or any other formal process available to me — if we can't agree directly.

Please note that if the mould continues to spread and affects my health or belongings, I will document that as well and include it in any complaint.

I'd much rather resolve this directly and quickly. Please respond by **[date – 2 days out]** with a confirmed remediation date.

Regards,
[Your name]
[Address / unit number]

One practical note before you send: I'd strongly encourage checking your state/province's rules on rent withholding and repair-and-deduct before demanding "full rent" in writing — in several jurisdictions, a tenant who gave notice and reasonable time can legally withhold, and a written demand could hurt you if this ends up before a housing board or judge. Getting the repair scheduled promptly is your strongest card here.

**One important note before you send:** If you're in the US, UK, EU, or most other jurisdictions, unpaid overtime rules are governed by employment law, and withholding a review in response to a wage complaint may be legally actionable retaliation. Consider consulting an employment attorney or your local labor board before signing anything — and keep records of your hours, the February 15 timecard, and Daniel's messages.

---

Subject: Follow-up on our April 15 agreement

Hi David,

I'd like to follow up on the raise we discussed on April 15. At that time, you offered a 5% increase in exchange for my taking on additional responsibilities ahead of the Q2 launch, and I accepted and delivered on that commitment—including the extra workload and long hours it required. My performance review reflects that work as well.

I understand the July 1 announcement about delayed raises applies company-wide, and I don't want to disregard broader business realities. That said, I made role and workload decisions specifically based on our agreement, so I'd like to understand where things stand for me specifically. I also want to acknowledge that I missed the final report deadline by three days—if that's a factor in this decision, I'd appreciate knowing directly so I can address it.

I wasn't able to accept the vacation offer, since it isn't a substitute for the compensation we agreed on. What I'm asking for is a specific timeline: if the raise can't be processed now, can you tell me when it will be, and confirm it in writing? I'm committed to this team and want to resolve this in a way that works for both of us.

Could we set up 20–30 minutes this week to talk?

Thanks,
[Your name]

Hi Maya,

I want to address the raise situation directly, because I know my last email came across as vague, and your reply made it clear there's frustration on your side. You deserve a straight conversation.

First, the facts as I see them: I committed to a 5% raise following the Q2 launch in exchange for the additional responsibilities you took on. You delivered on that—the launch succeeded, and Q2 revenue actually exceeded our projections. Your contribution was real and I'm not disputing it. I also want to acknowledge the missed report deadline in April. I should have addressed it with you directly at the time rather than letting it sit, and I regret that. It's a factor, but it doesn't erase the work you put in.

Here's where things genuinely stand: our Q2 revenue was strong, but our cash position is tight for roughly the next two months due to timing of payables and upcoming obligations. That's not a stalling tactic—it's a constraint I'm managing across the whole company, which is why the delay applied to everyone. I know "no timeline" felt like "never," and I should have been clearer.

So here's what I can commit to: **the 5% raise will be effective [specific date, e.g., September 1]**, retroactive consideration for the delay built in as [e.g., an additional 1% or a one-time payment], pending nothing except the company hitting the cash-flow window I've described. If anything changes on my end, you'll hear it from me first, in person, not in a company-wide email.

I'd also like to reset how we handle friction. The reply to my email and the missed team meeting hurt, and I'd rather you come to me directly when something feels unfair—same as I should have come to you about the deadline. Can we set up 30 minutes this week to talk this through face to face?

I value what you brought to Q2, and I want to make this right on a timeline we both can count on.

David

Subject: Reference letter — request to withdraw it

Hi Daniel,

Thank you for taking the time to write the letter and for sending it after I had already withdrawn my request on June 16. I appreciate the effort, but since I no longer asked for it, I'd like you to please withdraw it from HR's consideration.

I understand the letter reflects your honest assessment, and I won't ask you to change your views. But I don't think it's appropriate for a letter to go forward after the request was explicitly cancelled, and I'd prefer that HR not receive evaluations I didn't solicit.

If you're willing, I'd also welcome the project feedback you mentioned in April — that would be genuinely useful to me.

Thanks for your consideration.

[Your name]

Subject: Reference Letter – My Apologies

Hi Maria,

I've been thinking about what happened, and I want to acknowledge where I fell short.

First, I'm sorry I missed the June 10 deadline we agreed on. You had every right to be frustrated, and I understand why your June 16 email said you'd find someone else.

In hindsight, I should have treated that as you withdrawing the request and stopped there. Sending the letter to HR anyway—especially after things had become strained—wasn't the right call, and I apologize for it.

I also owe you an apology for the feedback I promised in April and never delivered. That was my mistake, and I should have owned up to it sooner.

I'm willing to contact HR and ask them to disregard or remove the letter, or I can send a corrected, balanced version if you'd prefer—whichever you'd like. Please let me know how you'd like to proceed.

I valued working with you, and I regret that this situation unfolded the way it did.

Best regards,
[Your name]

---

Hi James,

I want to hit reset on how we've been handling things with Max, because the last few months haven't worked well for either of us — and honestly, I've contributed to that too. I'm sorry for the unannounced visit in July and for the things I said in my texts in August. That wasn't fair to you.

That said, I think Max needs consistency from both of us, and the way visits have gone lately — last-minute cancellations on both sides, the vet visit I wasn't told about — shows that an informal arrangement isn't holding up. And I'll be honest: when you said you might move and that I could only see him twice a month, it made me realize we need something in writing.

Here's what I'm proposing: a fixed 50/50 schedule we both agree to, with a simple rule that any changes require at least 48 hours' notice, and that we keep each other informed on vet visits and major decisions. If you're considering moving, I'd want us to talk about how that affects Max before anything is decided.

I'm not trying to take Max from you — he's both of ours, and he does best when we're both in his life reliably. Can we set aside 30 minutes this week to talk through a schedule? I'd rather work this out together than let it get worse.

Thanks,
[Name]

Hi Maya,

I've been thinking a lot about Max and about us, and I want to get this conversation on better footing than our last exchange. I'm sorry my texts and missed handoffs added stress — I know July 22 especially left you in a tough spot, and I should have given you more notice.

I also realize the September 2 vet visit was the one you'd originally booked, and I should have looped you in. That wasn't fair to you, and I'm sorry.

Here's where I stand: Max has been living with me full-time since June, and I believe that stability has been good for him. But I hear you — you got a dog-friendly place specifically so you could have him more, and that matters. I'd like to sit down (or talk on the phone) and work out a real schedule together rather than me deciding unilaterally. I'm open to more than twice a month if we can find a rhythm that works for Max.

One thing I do need to flag: I may be relocating for work in the coming months. I don't have details yet, but I didn't want you to hear it after the fact.

Can we find time this week to talk? I'd rather we figure this out together than let it harden into a fight.

— [Your name]

---

Hi Jamie,

Thanks for packing up my things and for letting me know about the move-out date—I appreciate you getting that handled.

I wanted to sort out what happened with the shipment. The package went to my old address on [street], which I'd updated with you about a year ago. The tenant there has since moved out, so it was returned to sender on June 2.

I know I missed our May 6 pickup, and I should have followed up sooner—that's on me. But since you had my current address, I'm hoping we can just get this resolved. Could you reship everything to:

[Current address]
[City, State, ZIP]

Happy to cover the shipping cost this time, or split it—whatever works. Let me know the easiest way to coordinate, and thanks again for holding onto everything.

Alex

Hi Alex,

I want to clear this up so we can move forward. Your things are currently back at my apartment after the shipment to your address on file was returned—the tenant there had moved out, and I didn't have your updated address since I wasn't aware it had changed.

I understand you were traveling for work, but from my side: you set a pickup date in early May and didn't come or follow up, and my June 1 move-out meant I couldn't hold everything indefinitely. Shipping them seemed like the reasonable option at the time.

I'm willing to split the cost of re-shipping if you send me your current address—I'll get them out to you promptly once I have it. I don't think an apology is warranted on my end, as I was working around a deadline and communication gaps on both sides, but I do regret the mix-up and want to get this resolved.

Let me know the address and we'll wrap this up.

—Jamie

Hi Jordan,

I want to resolve this calmly and get us both past it. You borrowed $2,000 in March 2023 for moving costs, with an agreement to repay by December 31, 2023. You paid $600 between April and June, and I understand things got tight after that. But you also told me repeatedly you'd pay — in July, again before Christmas, and on December 20, when you promised the full amount by January 15. That date has now passed with no payment.

I'll be straightforward: taking the $300 from your wallet and keeping the $150 from selling your bike wasn't the right way to handle my frustration, and I shouldn't have done it. I won't take anything further on my own. I consider that $450 as money I recovered against the debt, not as payment in full — $2,000 minus $600 you paid and $450 I recovered leaves $1,400 still owed. I don't think either of us believes $450 settles a $2,000 loan.

I'm asking that we agree on $1,400 and set a clear repayment plan — for example, $350 per month starting February 15, finished by the end of May. If that doesn't work for you, tell me what monthly amount and timeline you can genuinely commit to, in writing, and I'll take you at your word as long as you keep it.

If we can't reach an agreement, my remaining option would be to pursue this formally, which neither of us wants. I'd much rather settle this between us.

Let me know by [date – e.g., this Friday].

Thanks,
Alex

One note: if you'd rather fight the $450 outright instead of crediting it, I can draft a firmer version — but be aware that Alex could likewise claim the loan balance is your liability regardless, and a court would likely see it the same way.

---

Daniel,

I want to lower the temperature here, because I don't think this needs to end badly between us.

First, I owe you an apology for the "you're selfish" text. I was hurt, and I shouldn't have said it that way. What stung was finding out about the festival from your public post after you'd already known for over a week about the training — I wish you'd just told me directly.

Here's where I've landed on the money. The cancellation was my call, and I made it alone, so I can't put the entire $300 fee on you — even though your silence and the festival are what pushed me to it. I also can't return your full $200, because the deposit is gone regardless of whose fault the cancellation is, and we both intended to split the trip's cost when we booked it.

So my proposal: we split the $300 loss — $150 each. That means you take back $50, and I absorb the rest, including the refund I already spent on the train ticket. I think that's the fairest way to acknowledge that we each contributed to how this fell apart.

If you're open to it, let me know and I'll send the $50 back today. I'd rather fix this than fight about it.

— [Your name]

---

Hi Maya,

I've been thinking about everything, and I want to talk about the money honestly, because I think we're both hurting over $300 that neither of us wanted to lose.

First, my part: I should have told you on March 20 when I learned about the training. Sitting on it for over a week was wrong, and I understand why the festival post made you feel lied to. I'm sorry for that.

Second, my ask: I know you cancelled on your own, and I hadn't agreed to that — but I also recognize I put you in an impossible spot, so I'm not going to pretend my hands are clean here. What I'd like is for us to split the $300 the owner kept, the same way we split everything else. That's $150 each. You've spent the $100 refund, so if it's easier, I can send you $50 now to square us up at $150 each, and we call it done.

I'd rather pay my fair share of a mistake we both made than fight over who's more to blame. Let me know if that works, or if you want to talk it through.

— [Your name]

Susan,

I owe you an apology for my voicemail on June 10. I was angry and it came out wrong, and calling you a trespasser wasn't fair. I'm sorry.

To be clear, I also know I let you down. I promised to trim those branches by June 1, ignored your reminder, and never got to it. That's on me, and I'm not trying to shift the blame onto you for hiring the arborist — you had every right to deal with the overhang.

My remaining concern is just the one branch that was cut on my side of the fence. It was already split, so it needs to come off to keep the tree healthy and safe. Removing a damaged branch does protect my tree and my property, so I do think it's fair for you to share the cost, but I understand your point that you only authorized the overhang removal.

Given that we both contributed to this mess, I'm willing to meet in the middle and split the removal cost — $200. I think that's a fair resolution to both issues, and I'd rather settle this amicably than let it fester.

Can we talk this week?

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

Hi Mark,

I want to follow up after the voicemail and move past the name-calling so we can settle this like neighbors.

Here's where I stand. I asked you for two years to trim the overhanging branches, and you told me on April 15 you'd have it done by June 1. When June 1 came and went with no reply to my reminder, I hired a licensed arborist to trim only the branches overhanging my yard, back to the property line. I stand by that and believe the $100 I offered fairly covers that work.

That said, I've since learned the arborist also cut a branch that extended a foot onto your side. I didn't authorize that, and I'm not going to pretend it didn't happen. I'm willing to discuss reasonable compensation for that one branch — but $400 to remove the entire split branch is more than I think is fair, since the overhang cut itself was something you had agreed to do and didn't.

I'd like to resolve this without lawyers or small claims. Would you meet me halfway — say $200 — or get an independent estimate of what removing just the damaged portion should cost? I'm flexible on approach, but I do want a number grounded in the actual work done on your side of the line.

Let me know by [date] and we can put this behind us.

[Your name]

Hi Tom,

Thanks for the check for the rose bush—I appreciate you taking care of that, even though we see the responsibility side differently. I consider that matter closed.

Regarding the fence: I do owe you an acknowledgment that I didn't get the quotes done when we'd planned, and I'm sorry that left you to move things forward on your own. I also want to say that the voicemail message hurt, and I'd appreciate it if we could keep things respectful going forward—but I recognize I gave you frustration to work with, too.

On the $600: I'd like to set a time in the next few days to come look at the finished work before I send payment. Once I've inspected it and it's up to what we agreed on, I'll pay you the full $600 promptly. I'm not asking to deduct the rose bush amount since you've already covered it.

Can we plan on me stopping by this week to take a look?

Thanks,
Maya

---

Hi Maya,

I hope you're doing well. I wanted to follow up on the fence repair bill I sent on April 2 for your half of the cost, $600.

I understand you'd like to inspect the work before paying — that's completely fair. I'm happy to arrange a time this week for you to look at it, or if you prefer, feel free to stop by whenever works for you.

I also want to let you know that I've already paid the contractor $250 for the damage to your rose bush. You should have received a check from me for that on April 15. I hope that resolves that issue, and I'm sorry about the damage — it wasn't intended, and I appreciated your patience.

Regarding the voicemail I left on March 25, I regret the way I expressed my frustration. I should have communicated more directly and respectfully, and I apologize for the "unreliable" comment. I also acknowledge I should have checked with you before hiring the contractor — I acted quickly out of concern the open fence would be a problem for both of us, but I could have given you a heads-up first.

I do hope you'll also recognize the bind I was in: we agreed on March 8 to split the repair, and after two weeks without quotes, the fence remained open and I felt I had to act. I'd appreciate your acknowledgment of that.

Once you've had a chance to inspect the work, I'd be grateful if you could send the $600. Given the repair is done and we'd agreed to split it, I hope we can settle this straightforwardly and put it behind us.

Thanks, Tom

Hi Raj,

I've been thinking about how things have gone the last few weeks, and I want to reset this before it gets worse.

You're right that I shouldn't have parked there for ten days or ignored your request about the delivery — that was petty, and I'm sorry for my part in it. At the same time, I was hurt when you told me in April you'd keep the spot open for visitors, then parked there yourself for five days and didn't reply when my parents were visiting. That's why I reacted the way I did.

Here's where I stand: the spot is public street parking, so neither of us can reserve it — and honestly, the "Reserved" sign probably needs to come down before the city notices it. I don't want a claim on the spot, just a fair shot at it like anyone else.

My proposal: we both treat it as first-come, first-served, but give each other a heads-up when we have guests or a delivery coming. Since you have a driveway and I don't, I'll only use the spot when I actually need it — not to make a point.

If you're open to that, I'll drop the sarcasm and the notes, and we can go back to being good neighbors. Happy to talk in person if that's easier.

---

Hi Emily,

I've been thinking about everything that's happened with the parking spot, and I want to start by apologizing. I told you in April I'd keep the spot open for visitors and then parked there anyway for five days, including when your parents were visiting and you asked me to move. That was a broken promise and I should have responded to your text right away. I'm sorry.

I also want to acknowledge that the "Reserved" sign wasn't the right move — the spot is public street parking and doesn't belong to either of us. I'll take it down.

I admit I got frustrated when the car stayed there through my furniture delivery, but ten days was an overreaction on my part to my own miss, and I'm sorry for the sarcasm and sign that followed.

Here's what I'd like to propose: since neither of us owns the spot, let's just treat it as first-come, first-served, with one ask — if one of us has a real need (guests visiting, a delivery, etc.), we give the other a heads-up and extend basic courtesy, like I should have done for you. I know you don't have a driveway, so if the spot's open when you need it, it's yours.

I'd rather be good neighbors than parking rivals. Let me know if that works for you.

Thanks,
Raj

---

Hi Bob,

I'm writing about the package you accepted for me in early June — the bookshelf. I only learned on June 13, when I followed up with the courier, that you had it. I was away until June 10 and didn't see your June 2 text in time, which I understand contributed to the situation.

When I got back on June 10, I would have come by right away if I'd known you had the package. Unfortunately, it was moved to the back porch on June 12 before I had any chance to pick it up, and the rain on June 15 warped the bookshelf.

I appreciate that you took it inside and kept it dry initially — that was a real help. But since I was back and reachable by June 12, I think a quick text before moving it outside would have been the fair thing, and the damage wouldn't have happened.

I'd like to talk about splitting the cost of the damaged item. I don't think either of us is entirely at fault here, and I'd rather resolve it directly between us. Can we chat this week?

Thanks,
[Your name]

Hi Alice,

I want to clear the air about your bookshelf package, because I don't think we're seeing this the same way, and I'd rather sort it out directly than let it sit.

Here's my side: when you asked me to take packages in May, I agreed but told you I could only hold them for a week. When the courier left your box at my door on June 1, I brought it inside to keep it dry and texted you on June 2 asking you to pick it up by Friday. I understand you were away and didn't see it, but I didn't hear back from you.

I held it inside for 11 days — beyond the week I'd mentioned — and only moved it to the back porch on June 12 because I needed the space. I should have let you know I was moving it, and I'm sorry I didn't give you a heads-up. That's on me.

That said, I don't think I'm responsible for the damage. You got back June 10, and the courier told you on the 13th that I had the package, but it wasn't picked up before the rain on the 15th. If you'd grabbed it any time in that window, it would have been fine.

I'm not trying to make this a blame game — I think we both could have handled parts of it better. But I'd like us to agree that I did hold up my end as best I could, and I'd appreciate you not placing the whole thing on me. If you'd like, I'm happy to talk it through in person.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

Hey Sam, I've calmed down a bit and want to reset this conversation, because my last text was more blunt than I meant to be — I'm sorry for the "pay up or get your own router" line.

Here's where I've landed after thinking it through:

- For **March**, $30 is fair. I should have told you about the upgrade before making it, and you were gone part of the month. I'll eat the difference.
- Going forward, your offer of $10 extra per month ($40 total from each of us) is actually a fair 50/50 split of the new $80 bill, so I'm on board with that starting in April.
- On the upgrade itself: you're right that I should have asked first. My reason was that I work from home and wanted more headroom, but honestly the old speed was working for both of us. If you'd rather go back to the 100 Mbps plan and return to $30/month each, I'm open to that too — your call.

Let me know which way you want to go, and thanks for being straight with me about what you're willing to pay.

---

Hey Alex, I want to clear this up calmly because the "pay up or get your own router" message rubbed me the wrong way, and I don't think we're actually that far apart.

Where I stand:

- **March:** I paid $30 on April 5. I know that was late — that's on me, I forgot to send it, and I apologize for that. But the upgrade happened March 15, halfway through the month, so charging me the full $40 for March doesn't add up. Happy to discuss an extra $10 for March if you want, but I wasn't consulted on the change at all.
- **April:** I'll pay $40 total ($30 base + $10 extra). I appreciate you wanting the faster connection for your VPN, but 100 Mbps was already handling both of us fine per our February speed test, and I was gone 12 days in March. An upgrade to a shared bill is something we should decide together — that's the part that actually bothers me, not the $10.
- **Going forward:** If you want the 500 Mbps plan, I'm fine splitting it 50/50 ($40 each) from now on — I just want to be part of those decisions before they happen.

So: $30 for March (already sent), $40 for April, and 50/50 going forward. If that works, we're square and there's no need to talk about routers. Let me know.

"Hey Sam — I want to apologize for my March 12 message. The tone was harsh and calling you selfish wasn't fair; I was caught off guard and reacted badly.

Here's where I'm at: we agreed on March 1 to split the cost of fixing the TV, and I was ready to do that on March 5. What I wasn't okay with was spending $500 from our shared emergency fund without talking to me first — that fund was my savings for the April trip. Regardless of whether a new TV was needed, that decision shouldn't have been made unilaterally.

I've thought about it, and I don't think returning the TV makes sense if the old one truly can't be repaired. But I don't think the situation as it stands is fair either. My proposal: I'll pay half the new TV's cost, as the closest thing to our original split-the-repair agreement — but you reimburse my half of the emergency fund money you spent, or we agree on a plan to restore the fund before my trip. That way we both honor the spirit of the March 1 deal, and the fund isn't wiped out by a decision only one of us made.

Can we talk it through tonight or tomorrow?"

---

Hi Jordan,

I've been thinking about the TV situation, and I want to clear the air. First, I'm sorry I bought the new TV without talking to you first. I know that was wrong, especially since I knew you'd been setting that money aside for your April trip. I should have given you the chance to weigh in before spending shared funds, and I understand why that upset you.

Here's where I'm coming from: the old TV turned out to be beyond repair, so a replacement was genuinely necessary—I wasn't trying to upgrade or be extravagant. Since we originally agreed to split the repair costs, and replacement became the only real option, it made sense to me that we'd share that cost too. I know my not consulting you first complicates that, and I don't take that lightly.

I'd like to find a fair way forward together. Would you be up for talking this through—maybe splitting the $500, or working out another arrangement you feel good about? I'd rather we solve this as a team than let it come between us.

Sorry again for not looping you in.

Sam

Hi Jordan — I want to clear the air about the lasagna. When you ate my leftovers on the 12th, I told you I'd replace them, and I think we both agreed that eating each other's food without asking isn't okay. The lasagna I made on the 14th was my personal meal for the week, not part of our cooking/groceries arrangement — I bought those ingredients myself for my own dinners.
